s: C. Other fundamental-rights domains.
Right to travel.

Saenz v. Roe (1999) identified three components: (1) entering and leaving another state; (2) being treated as a welcome visitor, not a hostile alien (Article IV); and (3) for new permanent residents, being treated like longtime residents (Fourteenth Amendment Privileges or Immunities).
Durational residency requirements for basic necessities fail (Shapiro v. Thompson, 1969; Memorial Hospital v. Maricopa County, 1974).
A one-year requirement for divorce was upheld (Sosna).
Voting.
Voting is "preservative of all rights."
One person, one vote applies to congressional (Wesberry, 1964) and state legislative districts (Reynolds v. Sims, 1964).
Total population is a permissible base (Evenwel v. Abbott, 2016).
Poll taxes violate equal protection (Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections, 1966).
Election regulations are reviewed under Anderson–Burdick balancing: severe burdens get strict scrutiny, and reasonable nondiscriminatory regulations need only important interests.
Voter ID was upheld in Crawford (2008).
Bush v. Gore (2000) held that standardless recounts violated equal protection.
Access to courts.
There is no general right, but fees cannot bar indigents from divorce (Boddie v. Connecticut, 1971) or parental-termination appeals (M.L.B. v. S.L.J., 1996).
Criminal appeals as of right require counsel for indigents (Douglas v. California, 1963).
Education.
San Antonio Independent School District v. Rodriguez (1973) held there is no fundamental right to education and wealth is not a suspect class.
Plyler v. Doe (1982) nonetheless struck Texas's exclusion of undocumented children, applying heightened rationality.
Second Amendment.
District of Columbia v. Heller (2008) recognized an individual right to keep and bear arms, especially handguns in the home for self-defense.
It noted "longstanding prohibitions" (felons, sensitive places) as presumptively lawful.
McDonald (2010) incorporated it.
New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass'n v. Bruen (2022) rejected means-end scrutiny and extended the right to public carry.

When the text covers conduct, the government must show the regulation is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation, through "relevantly similar" analogues judged by how and why they burden the right.
United States v. Rahimi (2024) upheld disarming people subject to domestic-violence restraining orders.
The historical inquiry seeks principles, not a "historical twin."
Second Amendment (Bruen / Rahimi).
Does the plain text cover the individual's conduct?
Ask whether the person is among "the people," whether the item is an "arm," and whether the conduct is keeping or bearing.
If so, the conduct is presumptively protected.
The government must show the regulation is consistent with the principles underlying the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation:
compare how (the burden imposed) and why (the justification) with founding-era analogues;
1791 is the primary reference point, and the 1868 evidence is debated;
analogues need not be "twins."
